analysis.one_liner: Creates a mandatory national inspection and safety program for all seafood sold in the U.S., including imports.
analysis.headline: The bill never came up for a Senate vote: after bipartisan introduction and one subcommittee hearing, it died in the Commerce Committee when the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have built the first comprehensive federal seafood safety system. It set health-based limits on contaminants in fish, required testing and closure of polluted harvesting waters, mandated unannounced inspections of processing plants, created an inspection system for imported seafood, authorized mandatory recalls, and protected workers who report safety violations. It was prompted by a National Academy of Sciences study finding that seafood safety oversight was fragmented and incomplete.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of seafood, including people who catch and eat fish recreationally or for subsistence, would get stronger protection against contaminated shellfish and fish harvested from polluted waters. State health agencies would receive federal grants covering up to 60 percent of approved program costs, and seafood plant workers would gain whistleblower protections, including reinstatement and back pay if fired for refusing unsafe work or reporting violations.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes enforceable tolerances for contaminants in fish products and deems seafood out of tolerance, or harvested from closed polluted waters, unsafe for sale [S2][S3].

Requires a comprehensive inspection system for fish sold in interstate commerce, including unannounced plant inspections, sampling, registration of all processors and importers, and detention and condemnation of unsafe products [S2][S3].
Creates an imported seafood safety system with inspections at ports and in exporting nations, bans shellfish imports from uncertified nations, and requires country-of-origin labeling [S2][S3].

Authorizes mandatory recalls of unsafe fish products, civil and criminal penalties, and whistleblower protection for workers who report violations or refuse orders that would create a substantial danger to the public [S2][S3].

Funds CDC-based disease surveillance for seafood-related illness, public education and advisories for consumers, health professionals, and recreational and subsistence fishers, and a five-year research program on contaminated fishing grounds [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Seafood processors, importers, and fishing vessel owners would bear compliance costs from registration, record-keeping, inspections, and handling standards, which would likely be passed to consumers in prices. Taxpayers would fund the program, authorized at $60 million for fiscal 1993 and $70 million for fiscal 1994.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall on processors and importers of all sizes, and the bill's own findings acknowledge the goal of protecting markets for the seafood industry, so some costs would surface in consumer prices [S2][S3].

The program splits authority among the Secretaries of Health and Human Services, Commerce, and Agriculture, creating coordination and potential duplication problems with existing FDA and state shellfish programs that the bill tries to layer onto [S2][S3].

The bill bars requiring freezing or cooking of fish intended for raw consumption unless that is the only practical way to make it safe, leaving a gap for raw seafood products that food safety advocates could criticize [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit of closing known gaps in seafood inspection — particularly for shellfish from polluted waters and lightly inspected imports — is substantial and the bill was designed to build on existing FDA, NOAA, and state programs rather than start from scratch. The main costs are compliance burdens on a diverse industry that includes small processors and vessel operators, and a three-agency structure that could have been cumbersome. On balance the design attempts to limit disruption to fishing operations, but the cost side is real and would have partly reached consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Commerce Committee, which held one subcommittee hearing and never acted on it again, so the bill expired when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ernest Hollings introduced the bill on April 7, 1992, joined by six original cosponsors including two Republicans (Stevens of Alaska and Cohen of Maine) [S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S1][S5].
The only further action was a hearing before the Subcommittee on National Ocean Policy Study on June 30, 1992 [S5].
The committee never reported the bill, and it received no floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Seafood processors and importers benefit from the bill's death, since they avoided mandatory registration, unannounced inspections, recall authority, and penalties. Consumers remain under the fragmented pre-1991 status quo the National Academy of Sciences said should be strengthened.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship with two Republican cosponsors, but no vote was ever taken, so no party split on the merits is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to register with federal regulators, keep traceability records, submit to unannounced inspections, and comply with mandatory recalls and civil and criminal penalties. Its death left the industry under the weaker, fragmented inspection system that preceded it.

Vessel standards, harvesting closures of polluted waters, and shellfish area monitoring would restrict where and how fishing could occur, but the bill's findings acknowledge that unsafe products destroy markets for the honest majority of the industry. Vessel standards were drafted to minimize disruption to fishing operations.

The bill would have imposed port-of-entry and in-country inspections, banned shellfish from uncertified nations, and required country-of-origin labeling. Importers' costs would rise, though consumers of imported fish would gain safety assurances.

States could run federally approved inspection and shellfish programs with grants covering up to 60 percent of operating costs, plus technical and laboratory assistance. This would have shifted some enforcement funding onto federal taxpayers.
